explanation:
Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You would not be wrong to correct that picture if your mom and sister let people believe they’re very involved when they go months without seeing or even calling your daughter.

First, you’ve already done the work on your side: you kept bringing your daughter around and you tried multiple times to talk to them about spending more time with her. This isn’t coming out of nowhere.

Second, the real issue is your daughter is getting hurt. She’s old enough to notice the gap and ask why they don’t like her, and that matters more than protecting their image.

Third, they’re helping create a false impression by agreeing when people talk like they see her all the time and by posting photos that make them look more present than they are.

The other side might say calling it out in front of others is embarrassing or that their health and lives make regular contact hard.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels unfair; you were trying to look out for her health. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong because you said no to a 19-year-old’s small birthday treat and turned the ride home into a debate about her weight and calories. That’s why it reads as controlling, even if your intent was concern.

What could change that would be new concrete facts about what actually happened—for example, if she had asked you not to buy sweets for her anymore, if a doctor had specifically warned against donuts that week, or if she said or did something in the car that changed the situation.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get that you feel judged, and being irritated by noise doesn’t make you a horrible person. But the verdict stays: yes, you’d be in the wrong if you told your niece to “shut up,” because that phrase is harsh and aimed at a kid rather than setting a respectful boundary.

What could change my view would be concrete details about what actually happened or was said—for example, her age, whether she was screaming for hours, whether you first asked politely, or the exact words you planned to use instead. Specific facts like that could matter; feeling misunderstood by itself doesn’t change the verdict.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information about what actually happened—for example, a specific message where he admitted she was using meth around him, a date and details showing she was actively high during something serious, or exact words showing you gave one calm warning before any jokes and he responded in a way that changed the situation.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get that you’re frustrated and feel the judgment is too rigid. But the verdict stays: you were in the wrong mainly because you were cruel to him and then misled him about the invite instead of giving a clear no. Being annoyed is understandable; insulting someone and stringing them along is the part that makes it asshole behavior.

What could change my view is new concrete info about what actually happened, like: a specific thing he said or did that was threatening or abusive, a message where you clearly told him he wasn’t invited, or a date/example showing he’d seriously disrupted past events.

0 — you’re not the asshole.

From your account, there isn’t a clearly blameworthy action here. You looked up from your phone and your eyes landed on someone who was standing right in front of you; that alone doesn’t show bad intent. Nothing in what you described shows you kept staring, said anything, followed her, or escalated it. And while the group reacted strongly, that reaction by itself doesn’t prove you did something clearly harmful or acted in bad faith.

The other side might say it looked like you were checking her out on purpose, even if that wasn’t your intent.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You told your friend clearly that adding this new player was making the game less fun for you and changing the experience, and he kept doing it anyway. That matters because this was a long-running playthrough where you and your friend were already near the end, so bringing in someone far behind changed the pace and balance a lot. You also didn’t try to block them completely; you still let them use your server while you AFK, which shows you weren’t just trying to control everything. And if playing with them feels boring enough that you don’t even want to log on, stepping back is a reasonable response.

What the other side might say: refusing to play and saying you don’t like the new guy probably made things more tense, and they may feel you weren’t giving him a fair chance.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get that it feels harsh, especially since you meant it as a compliment. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong because you shared a private sexual detail about him in front of other people, and it embarrassed him and led to unwanted attention. Intent matters less than the effect here.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information showing he had clearly said before that he was okay with you joking publicly about his body or sex life, or that in that moment he explicitly invited or welcomed that comment. Without something specific like that, the verdict stays the same.

You are not the asshole for wanting to send a polite text asking your new neighbor to turn the meditation music down.

First, the noise has been going on for multiple nights and is affecting your sleep, so this is not a tiny one-time annoyance. Second, you did not jump straight to a rude complaint; you even suggested a simple, polite message after trying to figure out what the sound was. Third, if noise from his apartment is clearly carrying into yours for hours at a time, it is reasonable to ask him to lower it. Fourth, waiting forever to catch him in person is not necessary when a calm text can solve it faster.

What may work against you is the “from Utah though” comment and the serial-killer framing, because that comes off as unfair and prejudiced when he has seemed nice so far.

1 — You would be in the wrong if you personally told your manager she smells.

First, this is a very sensitive issue, and the way you describe it includes humiliating guesses about her hygiene and period, which makes it more likely to come off as cruel than helpful. Second, you already know it could embarrass her, and because she is your manager, a direct comment from you could make the work relationship tense fast. Third, this has already turned into coworker gossip, which is unfair to her; piling on with a personal confrontation would not fix that. Finally, if the odor is truly affecting work, it should be handled through proper workplace channels and in private by someone whose role includes giving that kind of feedback.

The other side might say that if the smell is affecting everyone, someone should tell her so she has a chance to address it.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. She changed the routine, and blow drying her hair about 40 minutes before your alarm is a real sleep disruption. Being annoyed about losing sleep does not make you wrong, especially when this was not an issue before. You are also not demanding anything unreasonable if you ask for a small compromise, like waiting a bit when possible while you also shift your alarm a little earlier. And by your own account, nobody broke a promise or rule here, so this is more about working out a new routine than blaming anyone.

Her side might be that mornings are the only practical time for her workout and getting ready, so she may feel she is just doing what works for the household.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

Your mom made the hot dogs without you asking her to, and then blamed you for “wasting food” when the timing no longer worked for you. That’s not fair. You also told her you had just brushed your teeth, which is a normal reason to not want to eat right that second, and yelling at you over that was unnecessary. This really comes down to her assuming you were ready to eat instead of checking first. At most, you could have avoided the mix-up by saying before your shower that you weren’t ready for lunch yet.

Her side would probably be that she was trying to do something nice and felt unappreciated when you didn’t eat it.

0 — you’re not the asshole.

Your mom did go back on what she originally promised. She said they would cover anything the car needed besides gas, and then when the turbo repair came up, she tried to count that basic repair as your Christmas present instead. That changes the deal after the fact.

Your comparison was blunt, and raising your voice didn’t help, but that doesn’t make your main point wrong. You were reacting to a broken promise about a car expense you had already warned could happen.

It also matters that she raised her voice too, so this was an argument that escalated on both sides, not just you attacking her for no reason.

She might say the divorce changed her finances and that she was trying to help however she could, even if it wasn’t what she first promised.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for being upset that your boyfriend waved her over and then spent about an hour talking with her while you were left out. Being stuck there on your phone while the two of them chatted would make a lot of people feel awkward and sidelined. It also didn’t help that, when you wanted to leave, he called your attitude “pissy” instead of recognizing why you felt excluded. The bigger issue isn’t that he spoke to his ex at all, but that he let it turn into a long hangout without making sure you were included or comfortable.

That said, he might say you should have said clearly, in words, that you felt uncomfortable instead of trying to pull him away and then shutting down.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

Your concern is based on real warning signs: he’s underage, his cigarette smoking is becoming more frequent, and your family has a strong lung cancer history. You are not trying to embarrass him for one small mistake; you’re thinking about a pattern that could get worse. It also matters that you have only considered telling your parents, not publicly exposing him or trying to punish him. And the fact that you’re unsure and questioning whether it’s your place shows you’re acting out of concern, not spite.

The main point is that increasing smoking, especially with that family history, is not a harmless thing to ignore.

Your brother might say it’s his business, that he’s leaving soon anyway, and that telling your parents would feel like betrayal.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You stepped up in a very hard situation and spent a lot of time helping your dad with supervision and meals when the hospital could not give him constant one-on-one attention. That is not causing the family rupture; it is trying to meet his immediate needs.

Your sister’s response is a big reason this blew up. Calling your caregiving “stupid” and saying she should not have to help because she would rather do leisure activities is not a constructive way to handle a dying parent’s care.

It also matters that, by your account, she persuaded your mom to stop helping, and then your mom cut off communication with you. That breakdown did not come from you asking for help; it came from them refusing to engage fairly.

They might say they are overwhelmed, exhausted, or feel the level of care being asked for is too much for them.

0 — you were not in the wrong for asking your mum to tell you upfront what time she can actually drive you.

First, your request was practical: if she already knows she can only take you at 8, it makes more sense to say that first instead of asking what train you want and then changing it. Second, this seems to happen regularly, so you were reacting to a pattern, not inventing a problem over one day. Third, what you asked for was simple and reasonable: clearer communication in advance so you can plan properly. The only part that didn’t help was telling your sister to “suck a cabbage,” because that turned a fair point into an argument.

Your mum or sister might say your tone came off sharp and that your mum is still doing you a favour by driving you at all.

0 — you were not in the wrong for explaining why the 200px icons looked pixelated when viewed enlarged.

First, your employer was rejecting work based on a misunderstanding of how small graphics look when zoomed in, so giving a technical explanation was relevant. Second, the issue was blocking the work, so you needed to clarify it to move the project forward. Third, you were explaining the actual size and display limits of the icons, not talking down to her just because she was a woman. Fourth, she ultimately forwarded the work to the front end, which suggests the explanation at least helped the process continue.

What the other side might say is that your wording matters: if “dumbed it down” came across as condescending, the tone could still have felt disrespectful even if the explanation itself was necessary.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You are not in the wrong.

First, you did not just shrug and ignore it from the start: you told your mom it was morally wrong to keep it from Cathy, and you brought it up again later. Second, this was never your medical news to deliver in the first place, especially to people you barely know; that kind of talk is better coming from the parent or the doctor. Third, once your mom did tell Cathy, Cathy brushed it off, which shows the real problem was not you staying silent. Finally, your choice was shaped by the fact that you had limited information, no authority, and no clear way to make them act even if you spoke up.

The other side might say that because the possible illness was serious and urgent, any adult who knew should have told Cathy directly no matter how uncomfortable it was.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for feeling uneasy about adding someone you barely know to a two-week international trip. A long trip is a big commitment, and it’s reasonable to want the original group asked before another person gets invited. You were also honest about the real issue: you’re shy, anxious, and slower to get comfortable with people, not trying to punish this friend personally. And you didn’t turn it into drama—you said she seems nice and that you wouldn’t let your discomfort ruin the trip.

At the same time, this doesn’t sound like anyone else clearly did something awful either. Your boyfriend’s point that there’s time to get to know her is fair, but it also doesn’t fully answer the group-consent part.

The other side might say that if she’s kind and there’s still time before July, giving her a chance could make the trip better rather than worse.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not wrong for being frustrated. A few things make that reasonable: your neighbour knows your work and sleep schedule, yet the daily argument with the upset child happens right under your bedroom window; it’s not a one-off, it’s a repeated and predictable disruption that wakes you two hours early; and repeated sleep interruption would wear on most people, even if 7 a.m. is normal for the area. At the same time, there are practical steps on your side too: since you know it happens every morning, closing the window before bed would likely help, and if it keeps bothering you, calmly speaking to the neighbour is more useful than stewing in it.

The other side would probably say 7 a.m. is a normal time to leave with small kids and that morning tantrums are hard to control.

I get why this feels harsh, but the verdict stays the same: you were in the wrong mainly because you said you usually drive well above the speed limit and regularly pass on the right as your normal approach. That makes merging and lane changes less predictable, which is the core issue.

What could change my view is new concrete information about what actually happened, like your exact speed, the posted limit, whether a specific driver blocked the left lane for miles, dashcam footage, traffic conditions, or something specific that was said or done in one incident. General disagreement with the judgment isn’t new evidence.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

What would make me reconsider is a new concrete fact showing a real safety issue or lack of consent—like a specific message from her saying her parents manage her dating, a site rule requiring guardian contact, or something she said or did on the date that clearly showed she could not understand what was happening.

That’s more than ordinary human error.

What could change my view would be a specific new fact, like: you sent a message at 2pm that didn’t go through, she told you beforehand it was fine to stay late, or there was a concrete emergency or duty that kept you there.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

But the verdict is still that you’d be in the wrong, because you’d be excluding your brother’s spouse for being gay while keeping the homophobic relatives invited. The main issue isn’t your intent; it’s who is being asked to absorb the harm.

What could change that verdict is concrete new information about what actually happened or was said/done—for example, a specific threat from a relative, a past incident involving violence at an event, or proof that your brother’s husband himself caused serious disruption before.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

But the verdict still stands: you were in the wrong because you told her to wait and pushed a home workaround instead of prompt medical evaluation for a possible coin swallow in an 18‑month‑old. The key issue is the delay and replacing medical assessment with your own test.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information about what actually happened, like: the exact timing, whether a nurse/doctor/poison line told you waiting was appropriate, specific symptoms he did or didn’t have, or a message showing your wife had already confirmed he hadn’t swallowed it.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you feel dismissed: being kept on your birthday after getting prior approval was really frustrating. But the verdict stays the same: you were in the wrong because, whatever the pressure, you argued about a coworker’s injury and then deliberately damaged workplace property.

What could change that? Concrete new facts about what actually happened, like a specific message showing your manager revoked the agreement unfairly in advance, proof the injury was knowingly faked, or exact words/actions showing someone threatened you or physically blocked you from leaving before you broke things. Without that kind of new evidence, the core issue is still the destruction.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

What would change my view is new concrete information showing it was actually yours to use or that she clearly agreed—for example, a text where she or her parents said “you can keep the keychain,” proof it was bought for you, or a specific detail that you asked first and got a yes. Without that, the core issue stays the same.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong here: not for feeling hurt, but because you chose the unpaid extra work without telling her, it reduced the time you already had together, and then you brought that hidden sacrifice up in a way that put guilt on her.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete info about what actually happened, like a message where she asked you to make that arrangement, promised to match your effort, or knew about the unpaid hours and encouraged them.

0 — you were not in the wrong.

Your brother put his hands around your waist and buried his face between your shoulder and breast without asking, and you had every right to pull him off you. That kind of contact can feel very intrusive, even if he was just scared. Your reaction was sudden because you were startled and uncomfortable, not because you were trying to be cruel. Also, your twin saying you overreacted did not help; the better response would have been to calm your younger brother down without acting like your boundaries did not matter.

What the other side might say is that he is 13, got frightened by the movie, and was looking for comfort, so your shove and wording probably embarrassed him.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you feel judged harshly. But the verdict still stands: yes, you were in the wrong, because you chose an optional trip over being there for your 12-year-old’s actual birthday, and you also turned down the obvious compromise of shortening the trip to do both.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information showing this wasn’t really a choice in that way—for example, exact nonrefundable booking dates and costs made before you knew the birthday conflict, or a specific message from your daughter saying she truly wanted you to go and was fine celebrating later.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels unfair; the cancellation was frustrating and inconvenient. But the verdict stays: you were in the wrong because your main response was a profane message to the store, then arguing at checkout, not just being upset about the cancellation itself.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete evidence about what actually happened—for example, the exact text exchange, a screenshot showing they threatened or insulted you first, a written policy promising the free pizza regardless of customer conduct, or a specific statement from staff showing they singled you out for some other reason. Without that, the key facts still point the same way.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You told him clearly that this is not just general shyness, but anxiety tied to a specific fear: that this friend is close to his ex and could carry things back. That’s a real boundary to have.

You also didn’t blow up or forbid anything; you just said you don’t want to meet them right now. That’s different from trying to control his friendships.

And after you explained why, he kept trying to convince you anyway. His reassurances may be well meant, but they don’t erase your discomfort, and “she doesn’t hate you” isn’t the same as you feeling safe.

To be fair, he might say he’s trying in good faith to include you in his life and help you feel more comfortable around people important to him.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you feel cornered and judged. But the verdict still stands: you were in the wrong because, under pressure or not, you gave your boss a misleading version that could damage this person’s chances while hiding your own involvement.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information showing you didn’t mislead them—for example, the exact words you used to your boss, a message proving the interviewee knowingly pursued a married person, or a specific action by your boss that made clear refusal wasn’t a real option. Without a new factual detail like that, the judgment doesn’t change.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get that you feel the judgment is too rigid and that your intention was to limit the job by time, not dump extra work on him.

But the verdict stays: you were in the wrong because you knowingly gave false details in the booking, and only showed the extra rooms after he arrived. That put him in a misleading situation, even if you said he didn’t have to finish everything.

What would make me reconsider is a concrete fact showing he was told the real size beforehand and agreed anyway, like a message in the app, the listing saying “time-based cleaning regardless of room count,” or proof you accurately disclosed the upstairs rooms before booking.

0 — you’re not the asshole.

It’s reasonable to dislike people posting the same meme across multiple subreddits when it clogs your feed with the same thing two or three times. If you follow several meme communities, that repeated cross-posting can feel like low-effort spam rather than new content. You’re also not wrong for thinking people shouldn’t do it just to chase more views, especially when it makes the experience worse for people who follow those spaces.

That said, simply not liking it is different from being in the wrong. Your annoyance makes sense because the repetition affects your own feed directly.

The other side would probably say they’re just trying to reach different audiences, and not everyone follows all the same subreddits.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why the tone feels harsh, especially since you did ask before going. But the verdict stays the same: yes, you’d still have been in the wrong, because the main issue was planning to bring kids diagnosed with the flu to a family Christmas only four days later, despite the risk of contagion.

What would make me reconsider isn’t tone—it would be a new concrete fact about what happened, like a doctor specifically telling you they were no longer contagious by Christmas Day, negative flu test results right before the gathering, or that you had already decided not to attend before your sister raised concerns.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. Your friend was the one out of line here, not you.

First, it’s your home and you were not cutting people off from emergencies or basic contact, since everyone had normal phone service and data. Second, the real issue was your friend repeatedly ranting about it and then turning one guest’s casual comment into a public scene at your party. Third, it got tense enough that another guest stepped in with a hotspot just to calm things down, which says a lot about who was making the night uncomfortable. Finally, you listened to the feedback, admitted you hadn’t communicated well, and already decided to consider guest wifi going forward, which is a reasonable response.

The other side might say wifi is a normal courtesy now and that your rule felt unnecessarily rigid or odd to guests.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

You’re not the asshole for being upset that you came home after a brutal workday and 23-hour drive to no dinner, undone dishes, and being told to cook when the stay-at-home arrangement was supposed to cover that stuff. She had agreed to handle the home and kids while you were away, so your frustration was reasonable. It also makes sense that being exhausted and seeing chores half-done pushed you over the edge. And when she answered by saying you were “being an ass” because you’re gone, that added fuel instead of addressing the problem.

That said, calling her a lazy female dog and dragging the moving issue into the fight made it worse, even if you regret it.

Her side would be that early pregnancy, morning sickness, and handling two kids alone can leave her overwhelmed, so she may feel you judged her at her worst moment.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

But based on what you originally shared, you’re still not the asshole: the main reason is that these friends repeatedly make jokes at your expense about your school and living situation, and that leaves you feeling worse after seeing them.

What would make me reconsider is new, specific information about what actually happened—for example, a direct quote showing the jokes weren’t insulting, a message where you misrepresented why you canceled, a date/pattern showing you agreed to important plans and bailed last minute, or something concrete they said or did that changes the context.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information showing she actually crossed a clear line, like a specific date/message where she told the kids not to listen to you, called herself their mother, hid contact, made a medical/school decision against your wishes, or Jim/Sally ignored an agreed boundary you had already clearly set.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

Details like that could change the judgment.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

What would make me reconsider is a new concrete fact, like a specific email or statement from her approving those practices, proof she was told and ignored it, or that she directly invited a discussion about the company’s ethics at the event.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information showing it wasn’t deliberate or deceptive, like: he had already given you his name/contact, he told a mutual friend to connect you, you sent him a direct honest message right away, or the “coincidence” line wasn’t actually said. Without something specific like that, the judgment stays.

You are not the asshole.

You asked privately instead of springing the joke on them in public, which matters. When your friend and his fiancée said they’d prefer a new speech, you listened and changed course, so you didn’t push an insensitive idea after getting their answer. That also shows the real issue was never the joke itself, but whether the couple wanted it, and you respected that. On top of that, keeping any callback small and writing something new is a much better fit for a wedding where the bride was actually part of the first one.

The other side might say that reusing the whole speech would have made the day feel awkward, repetitive, and too focused on the failed marriage instead of this new one.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

What would make me reconsider is new, concrete information about what actually happened—for example: a time you knowingly shared a drink while a sore was active, a message where someone asked directly and you lied, or a doctor’s diagnosis plus advice you ignored. Without a specific fact like that, the verdict doesn’t change.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. Your mom is the one being unreasonable here, not you.

First, shutting off the home internet every night at 10 PM, including the last week of your summer break, takes away your free time for no clear reason. Second, waking you up early when you don’t need to be up is also controlling, especially during vacation. Third, based on what you wrote, this doesn’t sound like a response to you breaking a rule, missing school, or not keeping an agreement. And starting the bedtime rule again a full week before school makes it feel more about control than about school preparation.

Your side makes sense: you’re asking for a bit more say over your own schedule, not saying you should have no limits at all.

Your mom might say she’s trying to set a routine before school starts and make sure you get enough sleep.

0 — you are not the asshole.

You forgot the footpath rule and had already walked ahead, so you were not the person managing the situation when the collision happened. Your main concern was your son being hit and upset, which is a normal reaction, especially during an already emotional family moment. The person who was actually with your son at the time was your husband, so the mistake about being on the wrong side was not really yours in that moment. Also, once a child has been knocked over or hurt, basic decency is to check on the child first, not start yelling.

That said, your husband being on the wrong side of the path likely helped create the risk, and arguing over who was technically on the wrong side right then would not have helped.

The other side might say the path rules matter and that being in the wrong lane made things dangerous for cyclists.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong, mainly because you yelled and told your pregnant wife you had a right to weigh in on her eating because she’s carrying your child. With her already limiting it to a spoonful every few days, that comes across as policing, not just concern.

What could change that would be new concrete facts about what actually happened: for example, a doctor’s specific warning, the exact words either of you used, or a clear detail showing you didn’t raise your voice or try to control her choices.
